front_blocks.md: How is **oxygen** transported by red blood cells?

back_blocks.md: Oxygen binds to **haemoglobin** to form **oxyhaemoglobin**.
Each haemoglobin molecule can carry up to **four** oxygen molecules.

front_blocks.md: Define **carbonic anhydrase**.

back_blocks.md: **Carbonic anhydrase** is an enzyme in red blood cells that catalyses the reaction of **carbon dioxide with water** to form carbonic acid.

cards.front_md: Define **carbonic anhydrase**.
cards.back_md: **Carbonic anhydrase** is an enzyme in red blood cells that catalyses the reaction of **carbon dioxide with water** to form carbonic acid.

front_blocks.md: How does **carbonic anhydrase** help transport carbon dioxide?

back_blocks.md: It catalyses: CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
The carbonic acid then dissociates into **H^+^** ions and **hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO~3~^-^)**.

front_blocks.md: What is **haemoglobinic acid** and how does it form?

back_blocks.md: The **H^+^** ions released from carbonic acid bind to **haemoglobin**, forming **haemoglobinic acid**.
This buffers the H<sup>+</sup>, preventing a harmful fall in blood pH.

front_blocks.md: Define **carbaminohaemoglobin**.

back_blocks.md: **Carbaminohaemoglobin** is the compound formed when **carbon dioxide binds directly** to haemoglobin.

Most carbon dioxide is carried bound directly to haemoglobin.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Most carbon dioxide is carried as **hydrogencarbonate ions**; only some binds directly as **carbaminohaemoglobin**.

front_blocks.md: Define the **chloride shift**.

back_blocks.md: The **chloride shift** is the movement of **chloride ions (Cl^-^) into** the red blood cell as **hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO~3~^-^) diffuse out**.

cards.front_md: Define the **chloride shift**.
cards.back_md: The **chloride shift** is the movement of **chloride ions (Cl^-^) into** the red blood cell as **hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO~3~^-^) diffuse out**.

front_blocks.md: Why does the **chloride shift** occur?

back_blocks.md: As **HCO~3~^-^** ions diffuse out of the red blood cell into the plasma, **Cl^-^** ions move in to **balance the charge**.

cards.front_md: Why does the **chloride shift** occur?
cards.back_md: As **HCO~3~^-^** ions diffuse out of the red blood cell into the plasma, **Cl^-^** ions move in to **balance the charge**.

front_blocks.md: Why is the **chloride shift** important?

back_blocks.md: It **maintains the electrical neutrality** of the red blood cell.
This allows carbon dioxide to keep being transported efficiently.

front_blocks.md: In what **three ways** is carbon dioxide transported in the blood?

back_blocks.md: As **hydrogencarbonate ions** in the plasma (most).
As **carbaminohaemoglobin** (bound to haemoglobin).
**Dissolved** directly in the plasma (a small amount).

front_blocks.md: How do **hydrogencarbonate ions** come to be in the plasma?

back_blocks.md: Inside red blood cells, CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, which dissociates into H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>.
The **HCO~3~^-^** ions then diffuse **out into the plasma**.

cards.front_md: How do **hydrogencarbonate ions** come to be in the plasma?
cards.back_md:
Inside red blood cells, CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, which dissociates into H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>.

The **HCO~3~^-^** ions then diffuse **out into the plasma**.

front_blocks.md: What happens to plasma **hydrogencarbonate ions** at the lungs?

back_blocks.md: They re-enter the red blood cells and recombine with H<sup>+</sup> to form **carbon dioxide and water**.
The carbon dioxide is then **exhaled**.

back_blocks.md: The **partial pressure of oxygen** is a measure of the concentration of oxygen present — the pressure it contributes in a mixture of gases.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **shape** of the oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin.

back_blocks.md: It is **S-shaped (sigmoid)**.

front_blocks.md: **Explain** why the oxygen dissociation curve is S-shaped.

back_blocks.md: Binding of the **first oxygen** changes the shape of haemoglobin (a conformational change).
This makes it **easier** for the next oxygen molecules to bind — known as **cooperative binding**.

cards.front_md: **Explain** why the oxygen dissociation curve is S-shaped.
cards.back_md:
Binding of the **first oxygen** changes the shape of haemoglobin (a conformational change).

This makes it **easier** for the next oxygen molecules to bind — known as **cooperative binding**.

front_blocks.md: What does the curve show at the **high pO~2~** found in the lungs?

back_blocks.md: Haemoglobin has a **high affinity** for oxygen and becomes **almost fully saturated** — it **loads** oxygen.

front_blocks.md: What does the curve show at the **low pO~2~** found in respiring tissues?

back_blocks.md: Haemoglobin has a **lower affinity** for oxygen and its saturation falls — it **unloads (releases)** oxygen to the tissues.

cards.front_md: What does the curve show at the **low pO~2~** found in respiring tissues?

front_blocks.md: Define the **Bohr shift**.

back_blocks.md: The **Bohr shift** is the effect of an increased **carbon dioxide** concentration causing haemoglobin to **release oxygen more readily**.

cards.front_md: Define the **Bohr shift**.
cards.back_md: The **Bohr shift** is the effect of an increased **carbon dioxide** concentration causing haemoglobin to **release oxygen more readily**.

front_blocks.md: In which **direction** does the oxygen dissociation curve move during the Bohr shift, and why?

back_blocks.md: It shifts to the **right**.
Higher carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin's **affinity** for oxygen.

cards.front_md: In which **direction** does the oxygen dissociation curve move during the Bohr shift, and why?
cards.back_md:
It shifts to the **right**.

Higher carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin's **affinity** for oxygen.

front_blocks.md: How does **carbon dioxide** cause the Bohr shift?

back_blocks.md: Carbon dioxide forms **carbonic acid**, releasing **H^+^** ions.
The H<sup>+</sup> ions bind to haemoglobin, lowering its affinity for oxygen so more oxygen is released.

cards.front_md: How does **carbon dioxide** cause the Bohr shift?
cards.back_md:
Carbon dioxide forms **carbonic acid**, releasing **H^+^** ions.

The H<sup>+</sup> ions bind to haemoglobin, lowering its affinity for oxygen so more oxygen is released.

front_blocks.md: Why is the **Bohr shift** important?

back_blocks.md: In actively respiring tissues, carbon dioxide levels are high.
The Bohr shift means **more oxygen is unloaded** exactly where it is most needed.
